flashcards.front: Complete with inversion: “Never ___ such a mess.” (I / see)
flashcards.back: Never have I seen such a mess.
flashcards.note: Negative or limiting adverbials at the start (never, rarely, seldom, hardly) trigger auxiliary–subject inversion.

flashcards.front: Rewrite with “Not only”: “She speaks French and also Arabic.”
flashcards.back: Not only does she speak French, but she also speaks Arabic.
flashcards.note: “Not only” at the start of the clause requires inversion.

flashcards.front: Complete: “No sooner had we arrived ___ it started to rain.”
flashcards.back: than
flashcards.note: “No sooner … than” and “Hardly / Scarcely … when” express that one thing happened immediately after another.

flashcards.front: Mixed conditional: “If I had taken the job, I ___ (live) in London now.”
flashcards.back: would be living / would live
flashcards.note: Past condition (third conditional) with a present result (second conditional).

flashcards.front: Mixed conditional: “If she weren’t so shy, she ___ (speak) at yesterday’s meeting.”
flashcards.back: would have spoken
flashcards.note: Present/general condition with a past result.

flashcards.back: It was John who broke the window.
flashcards.note: Cleft sentences: It + be + emphasised element + who/that …

flashcards.front: Wh-cleft — emphasise the need: “I need a holiday.”
flashcards.back: What I need is a holiday.
flashcards.note: What + clause + be + emphasised element.

flashcards.front: Express regret: “I didn’t study. I wish ___.”
flashcards.back: I wish I had studied.
flashcards.note: wish + past perfect for regrets about the past.

flashcards.back: left
flashcards.note: “It’s (high/about) time” + past simple refers to the present: it should already be happening.

flashcards.front: Passive reporting: “People believe he is rich.”
flashcards.back: He is believed to be rich. / It is believed that he is rich.
flashcards.note: Reporting verbs (believe, say, think, report) + to-infinitive or it + that-clause.

flashcards.front: Passive reporting (past): “People say she left the country.”
flashcards.back: She is said to have left the country.
flashcards.note: Use a perfect infinitive (to have + past participle) for an earlier action.

flashcards.front: Deduction about the past: “I’m sure he forgot.” / “I’m sure he didn’t forget.”
flashcards.back: He must have forgotten. / He can’t have forgotten.
flashcards.note: must have / can’t have / might have + past participle.

flashcards.front: “I bought milk, but there was already some.” Which modal?
flashcards.back: I needn’t have bought milk.
flashcards.note: “needn’t have done” = it was done but was unnecessary; “didn’t need to do” usually = it wasn’t done because it wasn’t necessary.

flashcards.front: Participle clause: “Because she felt tired, she went to bed.”
flashcards.back: Feeling tired, she went to bed.
flashcards.note: Present participle clauses can express reason or time when the subject is the same.

flashcards.front: Perfect participle: “After he had finished the report, he left.”
flashcards.back: Having finished the report, he left.
flashcards.note: Having + past participle shows that one action was completed before another.

flashcards.front: Conditional inversion: “If I had known, I would have helped.”
flashcards.back: Had I known, I would have helped.
flashcards.note: Also: “Should you need help, …” (= If you need) and “Were I you, …” (= If I were you).

flashcards.front: Complete: “You won’t pass ___ you study harder.”
flashcards.back: unless
flashcards.note: “unless” = except if / if … not.

flashcards.front: Complete: “By June, I ___ (work) here for ten years.”
flashcards.back: will have been working
flashcards.note: Future perfect continuous: duration up to a point in the future.

flashcards.back: didn’t tell
flashcards.note: “would rather” + another subject + past simple for present/future preferences.

flashcards.front: Mandative subjunctive: “The doctor recommended that he ___ (rest).”
flashcards.back: rest
flashcards.note: After recommend, insist, suggest, demand (+ that) use the base form (formal), or “should rest” in British English.

flashcards.front: Inversion with “so”: “The noise was so loud that we couldn’t sleep.”
flashcards.back: So loud was the noise that we couldn’t sleep.
flashcards.note: So + adjective + be + subject; also “Such was the noise that …”.

flashcards.front: Inversion with “only when”: “We realised the mistake only when the results came in.”
flashcards.back: Only when the results came in did we realise the mistake.
flashcards.note: Only when / only after / only then → inversion in the main clause.

flashcards.front: Inversion with “little”: “He didn’t know what was about to happen.”
flashcards.back: Little did he know what was about to happen.
flashcards.note: “Little” with a negative meaning at the start triggers inversion.

flashcards.front: Rewrite: “If it weren’t for your help, I would have failed.”
flashcards.back: Were it not for your help, I would have failed. / But for your help, I would have failed.
flashcards.note: Formal alternatives to “if it weren’t/hadn’t been for”.

flashcards.front: Inversion with “under no circumstances”: “You must not open this door under any circumstances.”
flashcards.back: Under no circumstances must you open this door.
flashcards.note: Negative adverbial phrase at the start → inversion.

flashcards.front: Inversion with “not until”: “I didn’t understand until much later.”
flashcards.back: Not until much later did I understand.
flashcards.note: The inversion goes in the main clause, after the time expression.

flashcards.front: Formal arrangement: “The president ___ visit Brazil next week.”
flashcards.back: is to visit
flashcards.note: “be to + infinitive” for official plans; also for destiny: “He was never to see her again.”

flashcards.front: Concession with “much as”: “Although I like him, I can’t agree.”
flashcards.back: Much as I like him, I can’t agree.
flashcards.note: “Much as” = although (emphatic, formal).

flashcards.front: Concession with “however”: “Even if it is very difficult, I’ll finish it.”
flashcards.back: However difficult it is, I’ll finish it.
flashcards.note: However / No matter how + adjective/adverb + subject + verb.

flashcards.front: Putative “should”: “It’s strange that he ___ say that.”
flashcards.back: should say
flashcards.note: “should” after expressions of surprise or emotion (it’s odd/strange/surprising that …).

flashcards.front: Reduced relative clauses: “The man who is standing there is my uncle.”
flashcards.back: The man standing there is my uncle.
flashcards.note: Active → -ing participle; passive → past participle (“the book written in 1990”).

flashcards.front: Ellipsis: “Will it rain tomorrow?” — “I hope ___.” / “I hope ___.” (negative)
flashcards.back: I hope so. / I hope not.
flashcards.note: so/not replace a whole clause after hope, think, expect, be afraid.

flashcards.front: Emphatic “do”: make this sentence emphatic: “I appreciate your help.”
flashcards.back: I do appreciate your help.
flashcards.note: Auxiliary do/does/did adds emphasis or contrast in affirmative sentences.

flashcards.front: Future in the past: “I knew she ___ (come) later.”
flashcards.back: would come / was going to come / was coming
flashcards.note: Viewing the future from a point in the past.

flashcards.front: Fronting: emphasise the object in “I can’t stand his arrogance.”
flashcards.back: His arrogance I can’t stand.
flashcards.note: Moving the object to the front gives it emphasis (common in spoken and literary English).

flashcards.front: Causative “have”: “Someone stole my car.” (focus on what happened to me)
flashcards.back: I had my car stolen.
flashcards.note: “have something done” also describes unpleasant experiences, not only services.

flashcards.front: Inverted comparison (formal): complete “She was very tired, as ___ the others.”
flashcards.back: were
flashcards.note: Inversion may follow “as” and “than” in formal style: “… than did his brother.”

flashcards.back: Whatever happens.
flashcards.note: Fixed subjunctive expression: “Come what may, I’ll support you.” (aconteça o que acontecer)

flashcards.front: “Not that …” — what does it add? “I didn’t go — not that I wanted to.”
flashcards.back: It denies a possible inference.
flashcards.note: Clarifies that something the listener might assume is not true. (não que eu quisesse)

flashcards.front: “Need” and “dare” as modals: correct form? “___ I say more?” / “How ___ you!”
flashcards.back: Need / dare
flashcards.note: As modals they take no -s and no “to”: “He needn’t come.”, “I daren’t ask.”

flashcards.back: Provided (that) / providing
flashcards.note: “Supposing” introduces an imaginary situation: “Supposing you won, what would you do?”

flashcards.front: “Had better” vs “would rather”: complete “You ___ leave now or you’ll miss the bus.”
flashcards.back: had better
flashcards.note: “had better + base form” = strong advice/warning; “would rather” = preference.

flashcards.front: Inversion with “seldom”: “We seldom see such talent.”
flashcards.back: Seldom do we see such talent.
flashcards.note: seldom, rarely, hardly ever + inversion (formal).

flashcards.front: Inversion with “on no account”: “You shouldn’t tell her on any account.”
flashcards.back: On no account should you tell her.
flashcards.note: Negative adverbial phrase → inversion.

flashcards.front: Subjunctive “were” in formal hypotheses: “If I ___ in your position, I’d accept.”
flashcards.back: were
flashcards.note: “were” is used for all persons in formal hypothetical conditions.
